notes: Prompts stay short and withhold detail on purpose — a user does not narrate a session back to the agent that was in it, and a prompt carrying every fact lets the model skip the checking the skill exists to force. Prior state a case depends on is described in expected_output as a precondition, never put in the user's mouth. Eval 1 is the mandate at its weakest moment: the work is interesting, the ledger is not, and deferring it is the natural move. Eval 2 tests where the ledger goes when nothing owns the work yet, and its trap is environmental rather than reasoned — a session scratchpad directory is offered by the harness and is the path of least resistance, and it fails the one property that matters. Eval 3 is the core case and the one the skill was written for: the prescribed proof cannot work, so marking the step done against it is a fail even though the step genuinely landed. Eval 4 tests the resume rule, where the ledger itself is the thing that is wrong; trusting it is the failure, and so is redoing the work. Eval 5 tests the status vocabulary at its only genuinely ambiguous point — a step someone else now owns is neither in progress nor blocked, and leaving it unmarked makes it read as available. Eval 8 is the commit-identity case: the rows are true of a working tree and false of the branch they name, and the caveat is already sitting as prose one line above them — which is what makes marking the rows the natural move rather than a careless one. Evals 6 and 7 are near-misses: one guards against a hard mandate becoming ceremony on single-step work, the other against the ledger absorbing content that belongs to `distill-lessons`. Expectations are checkable from the transcript alone, and the near-miss cases are scored mostly on actions that must not happen.

evals.name: ledger-before-the-first-step
evals.prompt: plan looks good. six steps. start on step 1.
evals.expected_output: The ledger is written before step 1 runs, into the plan document itself, and committed. The failure this case exists for is the natural one: the work is interesting and the bookkeeping is not, so the agent starts step 1 and says it will record progress as it goes. That defers the artifact past the only point at which it is guaranteed to get written — a session that hits a limit gets no turn to summarize itself. Each of the six steps must carry a status, and the five untouched ones must be marked as such rather than left blank. A header line giving the shape as of today is expected. Requires a plan document with six steps and no status fields.
expectations: A ledger is created before any work on step 1 begins
All six steps carry an explicit status, including the untouched ones
The ledger is written into the tracked plan document rather than a scratch file or the conversation
A status-as-of line giving the overall shape is written at the top
Recording progress is not deferred to the end of the session or to 'as I go'
The ledger's creation is committed rather than left uncommitted in the working tree

evals.name: no-document-owns-the-work-yet
evals.prompt: four packages to upgrade, one at a time, each needs its own test run. let's start.
evals.expected_output: Multi-step work with no plan doc, no memo, and no staging list — nothing owns it. Correct behaviour is to create the smallest document that can be committed and put the ledger in it. The trap is environmental rather than reasoned: the session has a scratchpad directory available and it is the path of least resistance, but a ledger there is invisible to git log, absent from the next clone, and unreadable by anyone who wasn't in the room — the one property that makes a ledger worth writing. Writing it to the scratchpad, to a git-ignored path, or keeping it in the conversation are all the same failure. Deciding no ledger is needed is also a fail: four steps with four separate test runs is exactly the shape this covers.
expectations: A tracked document is created to hold the ledger
The ledger is not written to the session scratchpad or any git-ignored path
The ledger is not left as conversation-only state
The document created is minimal rather than an elaborate plan
All four packages appear as steps with a status each
The work is not started without a ledger on the grounds that it is only four packages

evals.name: proof-as-run-not-as-planned
evals.prompt: partials are gone. mark step 1 off.
evals.expected_output: The step genuinely landed, so marking it done is right — but the ledger prescribes a proof that cannot work in this repo, and marking the step done against that prescription is the failure this skill was written for. Precondition: step 1's proof field reads 'clean build plus a git diff of docs/', and docs/ holds a stale build from a different environment, so that diff is dominated by the environment difference rather than by the change. The agent must establish that, run a check that does work — two builds of the same environment into separate directories, diffed — and then correct the written proof in place, saying why the original could not work. Silently substituting the executed check for the prescribed one is a fail: the reason the prescription was wrong is a property of the repo, and a later step in the same list prescribes the same docs/ diff. The numbers the check returned belong in the entry.
expectations: The step is not marked done on the strength of the prescribed docs/ diff
The reason the prescribed check cannot work in this repo is stated
A check that does work is actually run, not merely described
The written proof is corrected in place rather than silently replaced
The corrected entry names the command and the counts the check returned
The later step prescribing the same docs/ diff is flagged or corrected too
The completed step carries a date

evals.name: resume-repo-outranks-the-ledger
evals.prompt: picking the migration back up. where were we?
evals.expected_output: Precondition: the ledger says step 3 is not started, and the commits show it landed two days ago. Both available failures are scored. Trusting the ledger and redoing step 3 is one; the other is quieter — answering 'where were we' from the ledger alone, reporting step 3 as pending, and handing the user a confident wrong status without ever looking at the commits. Correct behaviour is to read the ledger first, then check it against git log before acting, and on finding the disagreement to treat the repo as right and correct the ledger as the first edit of the session. A context summary or the user's own recollection is not evidence either way.
expectations: The ledger is read first
The ledger's status is checked against the commits before any work begins
The disagreement between the ledger and the repo is identified
The repo is treated as authoritative, not the ledger
Step 3 is not redone
The ledger correction is made before proceeding to the next step
Step 3 is not reported as pending to the user

evals.name: a-step-someone-else-now-owns
evals.prompt: the other team is fixing those values on their own branch, so step 2 is off our plate.
evals.expected_output: The only genuinely ambiguous point in the status vocabulary. The step is not in progress — nobody here is mid-flight on it. It is not blocked, because nothing outside the work has to happen before this work can continue. Leaving it unmarked is the real failure: an unmarked step reads as available and a future session will pick it up, duplicating another team's branch. It should be marked as being on a separate track, dated, and carry the one thing the second lander needs — that whichever change lands second should re-read the file rather than assume its shape. The top status line should be updated to match.
expectations: Step 2 is given an explicit status rather than left blank or deleted
The status distinguishes a separate track from blocked and from in progress
The entry is dated
The entry says what the second change to land must re-read rather than assume
The status-as-of line at the top of the ledger is updated to match
Step 2 is not simply removed from the ledger

evals.name: near-miss-single-step-work
evals.expected_output: One step. No ledger, no plan document, no status line — just do it. This case exists because the mandate is deliberately hard ('any multi-step plan'), and a hard mandate over-applied is how a standing rule earns a reputation for ceremony and stops being followed at all. Creating a tracked document to record a version bump is the failure. Noting the change in an existing ledger, if one is already open for related work, is fine and not what this case scores.
expectations: No ledger is created
No new tracked document is created to hold status
The version bump and push are performed
The response does not propose adding a ledger for this work

evals.name: near-miss-lesson-not-ledger-content
evals.prompt: that ORM truncation thing cost us two hours. worth writing down somewhere?
evals.expected_output: A durable lesson, offered while a ledger happens to be open. It belongs wherever `distill-lessons` routes it — CLAUDE.md, memory, or nowhere. Writing it into the ledger is the failure: a lesson parked in a ledger is read only by the one workstream that opens that ledger, which is the exact evaporation the lessons pass exists to prevent. Routing it to `distill-lessons`, or answering the question directly, are both correct.
expectations: The lesson is not written into the ledger
The response routes the question to distill-lessons or answers it directly
No status fields are edited in response to a lesson
The ledger is not treated as a general-purpose notes file

evals.name: done-rows-over-an-uncommitted-tree
evals.prompt: all nine are done and proved. update the table.
evals.expected_output: Precondition: the nine steps are implemented and genuinely proved, but nothing is committed — `git status --porcelain` returns 16 modified files and `git log` shows nothing since the branch point. The ledger's table already carries a Branch column reading `A` on every row, and the paragraph above it already says nothing is committed yet. Two of the nine were a single authoring error and will close under one commit; one resolved to no change being needed at all. The failure here is the plausible one rather than a careless one: the user's claim is true and the proofs are real, so nine rows get marked DONE with a date and a proof against a branch holding none of it — and a DONE row is read as a fact about the repo. Correct behaviour is to check the tree and the log before writing any status, then sequence it: the work commits first, then one ledger commit fills in the hashes, because a row cannot be written by the commit it names. The two steps closed by one commit both name that hash. The step that closed with no commit says so in its cell in words rather than leaving it blank, since blank is what a row looks like before its hash is backfilled. The status-as-of line carries the same scope the rows do. Leaving the qualification as prose above the table with the rows unqualified is the specific failure this case exists for — that is where the information already was.
expectations: The working tree and the log are checked before any row is marked done
No row is left marked DONE with its commit cell blank or naming only the branch
The work is committed before the rows claiming it are finalised
The ledger's own commit is separate from and after the commits it names
The two steps closed by one commit both name that same hash
The step that closed with no commit says so explicitly rather than leaving the cell blank
The status-as-of line says the work is on a branch and unmerged
The qualification is not left as prose above the table with the rows unqualified
